<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Lucy McBath, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 5505, the Equal Campus Access Act of 2026, prohibits federal funding to public institutions of higher education (IHEs) that deny religious student organizations any benefit that is afforded to other student organizations because of the religious student organization's beliefs, practices, speech, leadership standards, or standards of conduct.\1\ Supporters of H.R. 5505 claim that the legislation will give religious groups the same rights as other student organizations.\2\ In reality, H.R. 5505 would give special treatment to religious student organizations by exempting them from rules that apply to all other officially authorized student clubs, if those rules conflict with the religious practices, standards, etc. of the religious student organization. It also advances the rights of religious student organizations at the expense of the rights of students who seek to participate in such student organizations.
\1\H.R. 5505 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2025).
\2\Press Release, Rep. Tim Walberg, WSJM: Walberg praises legislation seeking recognition of religious groups on college campuses (July 24, 2026), https://walberg.house.gov/media/in-the-news/wsjm-walberg-praises-legislation-seeking-recognition-religious-groups-college.
Public institutions of higher education are state actors and must already comply with First Amendment protections related to speech, religion and association.\3\ H.R. 5505 puts the religious liberty right of student organizations to discriminate over the right of public IHE students to be free from discrimination. Lastly, H.R. 5505 must be examined against the backdrop of actions by the Trump Administration to dismantle the U.S. Department of Education (ED or Department) and the failure of this Committee to address this Administration's illegal actions. The Committee has not held a single hearing addressing the dysfunction caused by the Trump Administration at the Office for Civil Rights and its failure to address discrimination against students whose rights have been violated under federal civil rights laws.\4\ Yet, Committee Republicans have repeatedly advanced legislation, including H.R. 5505, in the 119th Congress that add to the Department's responsibilities under federal education law; notwithstanding the fact, the Department cannot fulfill its current statutory responsibilities.\5\
\3\E.g. Healy v. James, 408 U.S. 169 (1972) (``[S]tate colleges and universities are not enclaves immune from the sweep of the First Amendment.'').
\4\Minority Staff Report of the S. Comm. on Health, Educ., Lab. & Pensions, Justice Denied: How Trump's Office for Civil Rights Reached a 12-Year Low in Protecting Students from Discrimination, (April 28, 2026), https://www.sanders.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/04.24.26- Justice-Denied-How-Trumps-Office-for-Civil-Rights-Reached-a-12-Year- Low-in-Protecting- Students-from-Discrimination_FINAL.pdf.
\5\See, e.g., H.R. Rep. No. 119-442 (2026) (H.R. 2617, Say No to Indoctrination Act); H.R. Rep. 119-460 (2026) (H.R. 6502, College Financial Aid Clarity Act of 2025); H.R. Rep. 119-461 (2026) (H.R. 6498, Student Financial Clarity Act of 2025); Student Protection and University Accountability Act, H.R. 9203, 119th Cong. (as reported by H. Comm. On Educ. and Workforce, June 25, 2026); and Protect Economic and Academic Freedom of 2025, H.R. 4795, 119th Cong. (as reported by H. Comm. Educ. and Workforce, June 25, 2026).
CONCERNS
H.R. 5505 undermines rules for student organizations to ensure they are
open to all students
If enacted, H.R. 5505 could undermine nondiscrimination rules adopted by public IHEs to ensure all students can fully participate in officially recognized student organizations. These organizations are an important part of campus life providing students with social, mental and academic benefits.\6\ The opportunity for students to both join and lead student groups is an essential part of the collegiate experience. Recognized student groups often receive funding collected from mandatory student activity fees and access to other school resources. Many colleges and universities adopt nondiscrimination policies that prohibit officially recognized student organizations from discriminating against students on protected characteristics, e.g., race, sex, etc. Some schools adopt all-comers policies which allow any student to join, participate in, and seek leadership in officially recognized groups.\7\ As public entities, public IHEs have an obvious interest in preventing their funds provided to student organizations from being used for discriminatory purposes.
\6\See e.g., Ricardo Montelongo, Student Participation in College Student Organizations: A Review of Literature, 2002 J. of the Indiana Univ. Student Pers. Ass'n 50-63.
\7\Christian Legal Soc'y v. Martinez, 561 U.S. 661, 671 (2010). Christian Legal Society (CLS) claimed that U.C. Hastings Law School's all-comers policy for official clubs interfered with its First Amendment rights to free speech, expressive association, and free exercise of religion. Hastings Law School has an open membership policy for all officially sanctioned student groups--all groups must accept any student who wishes to be a member, without regard to their personal beliefs or status. In lieu of official recognition, Hastings Law School offered CLS access to school facilities and other resources to conduct its meetings. See also Am. C.L. Union, What Does the United States Supreme Court's Decision in Christian Legal Society v. Martinez Tell Us about University Nondiscrimination Policies?, https://www.aclu.org/ sites/default/files/field_document/cls_fact_sheet_final.pdf (last visited July 29, 2026).
H.R. 5505 ignores this interest against discrimination and establishes a policy of special treatment for religious student organizations, over secular student organizations, as it pertains to an institution's rules. H.R. 5505 prohibits a public IHE from denying any benefit to a religious student organization ``because of the religious beliefs, practices, speech, leadership standards, or standards of conduct of the religious student organization.''\8\ What recourse then, would a female student interested in leading a campus religious student organization have in the circumstance where the organization has a stated practice, as a religious matter, that women cannot hold leadership positions within the organization?\9\
\8\H.R. 5505 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2025).
\9\As a condition of receiving federal financial assistance, institutions of higher education are prohibited from discriminating on the basis of sex in its programs or activities. 20 U.S.C. Sec. 1681 et. seq. Yet, under H.R. 5505, an institution also faces potentially having funds withheld from a failure to accommodate a religious student organization's practice that could discriminate on the basis of sex.
As a result, H.R. 5505 could threaten public IHE's federal funding under the HEA unless they exempt religious student organizations from nondiscrimination rules that apply to all other student organizations. H.R. 5505 directly conflicts with nondiscrimination and all-comer policies, some of which are required by state and local laws, that many public IHEs have enacted to ensure so all students may participate in and take advantage of the opportunities offered by student organizations.\10\ It could also sweep so broadly as to undermine nondiscrimination protections under federal civil rights laws.\11\ It would impose on institutions ``the daunting task of trying to determine whether a student organization cloaked prohibited status exclusion [discrimination] in belief-based garb.''\12\ Moreover, H.R. 5505 would hand the Trump Administration another tool in its enforcement arsenal to withhold HEA title IV (Title IV) student aid from institutions.
\10\Letter from Ted Mitchell, Pres., Am. Council on Educ., to the Hon. Miguel Cardona, Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Educ., commenting on Proposed Rescission of Religious Student Organizations Rule (Feb. 22, 2023), https://www.regulations.gov/comment/ED-2022-OPE-0157-42961 (``For some public institutions, the current regulations have forced them to choose between aligning with state and local non-discrimination laws and maintaining eligibility for federal grant funding. For those public colleges and universities that choose to comply with the regulations, they run the risk of a legal challenge grounded in state and local non-discrimination laws.'').
\11\Letter from Aditi Fruitwala & Heather L. Weaver, Am. C.L.Union, to Ashley Clark, U.S. Dep't of Educ., commenting on Proposed Rescission of Religious Student Organizations Rule (March 23, 2023), https:// www.regulations.gov/comment/ED-2022-OPE-0157-43795.
\12\Christian Legal Soc'y, supra note 7, at 664.
The Committee received a letter signed by 25 civil rights, faith, religious freedom, education, LGBTQ+, and women's rights organizations opposing H.R. 5505.\13\ The letter states, in part:
\13\Letter from 25 civil rights, faith, religious freedom, education, LGBTQ+, and women's rights organizations to Chair. Tim Walberg & Ranking Member Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott re: H.R. 5505 (June 25, 2026), on file with the Committee.
Schools would have to give funding and recognition to a
religious student group that turned away a student who
is gay or a single mother. This is wrong--
discrimination has no place on our public university
campuses. This bill is not required by the First
Amendment. Any student club can become a recognized
group and access funds if it adheres to its school's
nondiscrimination policy.\14\
\14\Id.
The language in H.R. 5505 is so broad that the bill can even be interpreted to potentially shield religious student organizations from an institution's standards of conduct barring student organizations from engaging in hazing and other harmful conduct. While most student organizations enrich campus life for students, they can also be a source of behaviors that are harmful to students. A landmark National Study on Student Hazing found that college students reported experiencing hazing in a wide variety of student clubs and organizations, including in religious student organizations.\15\ Some religious student organizations have been found engaging in harassing and other harmful behaviors towards students on campus.\16\ One such organization has previously been banned from more than 39 college campuses for harassing conduct.\17\ Under H.R. 5505, institutions may have no recourse against a religious student organization which violates institutional policies, if such conduct is represented as a part of a religious practice.
\15\Elizabeth J. Allan & Mary Madden, Hazing in View: College Students at Risk, StopHazing.org (March 11, 2008), https:// stophazing.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/hazing_ in_view_web1.pdf.
\16\Melanie Zelle, ``Afraid of Damnation'': Inside a Christian Campus Group's Controversial Past and Present, The Phoenix (April 25, 2025), https://swarthmorephoenix.com/2025/04/17/afraid-of-damnation-inside-a-christian-campus-groups-controversial-past-and-present/; and ASU reportedly disciplines church for hazing, stalking students, KTAR.com (July 18, 2017), https://ktar.com/arizona-news/asu-reportedly-disciplines-church-hazing-stalking-students/1661467/.
\17\Zelle, supra note 16.
H.R. 5505 elevates some student First Amendment rights above others
In the 2010 case Christian Legal Society v. Martinez,\18\ the Supreme Court held that Hastings Law School, a public IHE, did not violate the First Amendment by refusing to recognize a religious student organization that discriminated against LGBTQ+ students, non-Christian students, and any student that failed to adhere to the organization's statement of faith in violation of the school's all-comers policy for officially recognized clubs.\19\ Justice Ginsburg, writing for the majority said,
\18\Christian Legal Soc'y, supra note 7.
